He wants to know which shop will satisfy his daily dose of caffeine faster. During the next 10 days, he decides to collect data after 5 visits for each shop at different times of the day. |  Visits | Order time at 1st shop (min) | Order time at 2nd shop (min)  |

|  2 | 2 | 1  |
|  3 | 1 | 1  |

question_text: Koshi-kun creates a new GMO sunflower plant which he claims to have better yield. Hamtaro wants to conduct a hypothesis testing experiment to figure out whether this new plant is better than the previous one. The old plant has an average yield of 1 Kg with a variance of 0.04. Each GMO plant cost 5% more than the original plant. How many GMO plants should Hamtaro grow? Assume a power of 0.5 and a significant level of 0.05.
canonical_solution:
The sample size is UNDERDETERMINED from the source information alone. Planning power requires a target effect size, such as delta=mu_target-mu_0: the mean yield improvement the experiment should be able to detect. The source gives mu_0=1 kg, variance 0.04 kg^2, hence standard deviation sqrt(0.04)=0.2 kg, alpha=0.05, and power=0.5 (beta=0.5). It does not give an explicit target GMO mean or minimum detectable yield improvement. A 5% higher cost is an economic fact, not automatically a 5% statistical yield effect.
Path A — complete underdetermination explanation: identify the missing detectable yield difference and explain that the known variance, alpha, and desired power cannot determine n without a specified alternative mean/effect. Different target improvements require different sample sizes; smaller improvements generally require more observations under the same model and error requirements. Even if the old-plant variance is provisionally used for the GMO plants, the missing target effect still prevents a unique numerical answer. Recognizing this, correctly interpreting the supplied standard deviation and error/power inputs, and concluding that a target effect must be supplied is eligible for full credit. No invented effect, exact formula, or numerical sample size is required for this path.
Path B — explicitly conditional example: as an EXTRA ASSUMPTION, suppose the 5% price premium motivates choosing a 5% minimum detectable yield improvement, with yield value proportional to kilograms and other costs unchanged. This assumption is not stated by the source. Then mu_target=1.05 kg and delta=0.05 kg. Also assume independent GMO yields with known/planning variance 0.04, a known historical baseline 1 kg, and a one-sided normal-mean test of H0: mu<=1 versus H_A: mu>1. Under this model,
power=Phi(delta sqrt(n)/sigma-z_(1-alpha)),
so n=[(z_(1-alpha)+z_(power))*sigma/delta]^2.
Substituting alpha=0.05, power=0.5, sigma=0.2 and the ASSUMED delta=0.05 gives n=[(1.644854+0)*0.2/0.05]^2=43.288695. Round up to 44 plants; power at 44 is about 0.50537. The source multiple-choice key's 45 is the nearest offered option and a valid conservative choice under these assumptions. Neither 44 nor 45 is uniquely implied by the question as written.
Accept another explicit defensible effect-size/model assumption and any statistically valid, internally consistent power calculation; do not require this particular formula or numerical answer. If the null instead tests whether mean yield exceeds the economic threshold 1.05 kg, a target alternative above that threshold must be specified for the corresponding power calculation: the illustrated test against 1 kg does not establish that yield exceeds 1.05. A silent substitution of a 5% effect cannot earn full credit, even if it happens to produce 44 or 45.

Because Hamtaro has many business ventures, he controls two social media pages on Hambook. The two pages are very similar in size and demographic. Both have one million followers and around 100,000 daily reach. The table below show the performance of some posts on the two pages.

|  Post | Reactions | Likes | Comments | "Read more" clicks | Share  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
|  1 Buriram United wins Thailand tournament | 34k | 2.3k | 632 | 1.1k | 1.2k  |
|  2 Dena Baystars wins Japan Series | 36k | 2.2k | 1050 | 1.2k | 1.0k  |
|  3 Saudi wins World cup bid | 23k | 2.1k | 2030 | 1.0k | 0.6k  |
|  4 Ichiran review | 35k | 1.0k | 3000 | 1.1k | 5.3k  |
|  5 Pangcha review | 32k | 1.2k | 203 | 1.2k | 5.2k  |
|  6 Are-Am-Eat review | 22k | 1.1k | 103 | 1.1k | 3.2k  |

Reaction includes likes, bookmark, and comments. Value is in thousands (k). Posts 1, 2, and 3 are sports related posts of similar nature. Posts 4, 5 and 6 are restaurant review of similar style. However, post 3 and 6 are low quality posts written by a junior writer using CHADGPT. A typical post gains 99% of the views in one day, and most users visit the page during lunch hour.

Elon Mark recently bought Hambook and changed its name to "H." With the name change he also introduced changes to the feed recommendation algorithm. Hamtaro notices that the performance of his posts decreases by a lot with this change (a reduction of 30% on all metrics). As the expert who is about to finish the Statistics part of Com Eng Meth II course, you should help Hamtaro out of this crisis. Koushi-kun hypothesizes that putting links in the comments instead of inside the post will help improve Hamtaro's situation. Help Hamtaro conduct an A/B test to verify this hypothesis.

What should be the metric used? Discuss the potential benefits or disadvantage of each possible metrics. To receive full credit, you should also justify your answer using concepts learned in this course.
canonical_solution:
Choose one primary outcome before the experiment and define the experimental unit and observation window. A defensible choice is mean 24-hour "Read more" clicks per assigned post, compared between link-in-post and link-in-comment treatments. It measures an aspect of content engagement with a window that captures about 99% of views. It is not automatically a count of outbound-link clicks or business conversions. If the business objective is external traffic, separately instrument outbound clicks/conversions and state that additional logging is needed; those data are not supplied. Per-post totals measure total performance; rates per impression measure engagement conditional on exposure, a different estimand because treatment may itself change reach.
Tradeoffs for the available metrics:
- Reactions: broad and usually plentiful, hence potentially sensitive to changes, but combine unequal types of activity, may include shallow/negative engagement, and overlap with likes/comments. Do not add these overlapping counts as if independent outcomes.
- Likes: simple, familiar, frequent positive-engagement proxy; low effort and may not reflect reading, link visits, or business value.
- Comments: richer interaction and discussion; may be driven by controversy, spam, or the link comment itself. A consistent rule excluding the page's own treatment-delivery comment avoids mechanical inflation.
- "Read more" clicks: closer to opening/reading the post and relatively similar across these examples; opening is not completed reading or an outbound click, and a small selected table cannot prove stability or treatment sensitivity.
- Shares: potential amplification and reach; strongly content/category dependent, potentially skewed/viral, and not necessarily evidence of positive sentiment or conversion.
The sports and restaurant posts show different engagement patterns, and posts 3 and 6 have lower stated quality. Block/adjust for category and quality; do not infer the link-placement effect from this nonrandomized six-post table. Avoid comparing raw counts across unbalanced exposure/opportunity without specifying the desired estimand. A prespecified primary metric with secondary/guardrail outcomes reduces cherry-picking and multiplicity; randomization supports causal attribution, and uncertainty must reflect the assignment unit and repeated audience exposure. Accept another well-defined primary metric when its benefits, limits, and relationship to Hamtaro's objective are justified. Do not fabricate per-post reach, impressions, or click-through rates from the page-wide daily reach.

Let mu_1 and mu_2 be population mean order times for the two shops under comparable target visit conditions. As a primary analysis, use H0: mu_1-mu_2=0 versus H_A: mu_1-mu_2!=0. The recorded visit numbers do not establish matching by time or day, so an independent-sample Welch t-test is a defensible default; equal population variances need not be assumed. Approximate t inference requires independent visits and roughly normal populations for these very small samples. The uncontrolled collection weakens both this model and any causal interpretation.
The sample means are 1.8 and 1.6 minutes. With n_1=n_2=5, sums of squared deviations are 2.8 and 3.2; sample variances are s_1^2=0.7 and s_2^2=0.8 min^2. Thus
SE=sqrt(0.7/5+0.8/5)=sqrt(0.3)=0.547723;
t=(1.8-1.6)/0.547723=0.365148;
nu=(0.7/5+0.8/5)^2 / [(0.7/5)^2/4+(0.8/5)^2/4]=7.964602.
Under H0, the Welch statistic is approximately t_nu. The two-sided p-value is about 0.724507. At an explicitly chosen illustrative alpha=0.05 (not specified in the question), fail to reject H0. A 95% difference interval is approximately [-1.064,1.464] minutes; equivalently |t| is below the approximately 2.308 two-sided critical value. There is insufficient evidence of different mean order times, or of shop 2 reliably being faster; this is not proof that the shops are equal. The observed 0.2-minute advantage for shop 2 is small compared with uncertainty, and possible visit-condition confounding remains.
Accepted alternatives: With an explicit equal-variance assumption, a pooled two-sample t-test has s_p^2=(2.8+3.2)/8=0.75, the same SE and statistic, df=8, and two-sided p about 0.724466. If a directional faster-shop-2 question was specified before looking at the means, H_A: mu_1-mu_2>0 gives one-sided Welch p about 0.362253; the 5% conclusion is unchanged. Reversing subtraction/hypothesis signs consistently is equivalent. Another stated alpha is acceptable when the decision matches it; alpha was not supplied.
A paired test needs an additional, justified matching assumption absent from the source; row numbering or the same visitor alone is not sufficient. Conditionally assuming genuine matched visits, differences (-2,1,0,1,1) have mean 0.2, sample variance 1.7, SE=sqrt(1.7/5)=0.583095, t=0.342997, df=4, and two-sided p about 0.748868. This is a possible mechanism, not a fact observed in the table. Merely visiting at different times does not guarantee balanced conditions.
Other unrecorded conditions could include day of week/date, queue length and customer arrival rate, staffing, barista workload, order size/complexity, or promotions. These can affect service time independently of a shop's underlying performance. Without recording, matching, blocking, or randomizing these conditions, a mean difference can combine a shop effect with a difference in demand or order conditions. Define the measured interval consistently (queue-to-order completion or another fixed start/end); the table's 'order time' does not specify every measurement detail.
The same hamster provides only five visits per shop in ten days, so precision is low and generalization to other times, customers, and orders is limited. Small sample size itself mainly increases uncertainty; it is not proof of systematic bias. Visit numbers are not evidence of matched same-day/same-condition pairs, and repeated visits may have dependence. The data do not prove any named confounder actually occurred. question_text: We observed that, from 1am to 4am, the number of shooting stars in each hour is 8, 4, 3. Assuming that the rate of the falling star follow a Poisson distribution, find the MLE $\hat{\lambda}$.
canonical_solution:
Treat the three non-overlapping one-hour counts as independent Poisson(lambda) observations with constant hourly rate lambda. The likelihood is
L(lambda)=product [exp(-lambda)lambda^{x_i}/x_i!]=exp(-3lambda)lambda^15/(8!4!3!).
The log likelihood is -3lambda+15 log(lambda)-log(8!4!3!), giving derivative -3+15/lambda=0 and lambda_hat=15/3=5. The second derivative is -15/lambda^2<0, so this is a maximum. Directly invoking the known Poisson MLE lambda_hat=sample mean is equally valid; no differentiation is required. The estimated rate is five shooting stars per hour.

question_text: Koshi-kun creates a new GMO sunflower plant which he claims to have better yield. Hamtaro wants to conduct a hypothesis testing experiment to figure out whether this new plant is better than the previous one. The old plant has an average yield of 1 Kg with a variance of 0.04. Each GMO plant cost 5% more than the original plant. How many GMO plants should Hamtaro grow? Assume a power of 0.5 and a significant level of 0.05.
canonical_solution:
The sample size is UNDERDETERMINED from the source information alone. Planning power requires a target effect size, such as delta=mu_target-mu_0: the mean yield improvement the experiment should be able to detect. The source gives mu_0=1 kg, variance 0.04 kg^2, hence standard deviation sqrt(0.04)=0.2 kg, alpha=0.05, and power=0.5 (beta=0.5). It does not give an explicit target GMO mean or minimum detectable yield improvement. A 5% higher cost is an economic fact, not automatically a 5% statistical yield effect.
Path A — complete underdetermination explanation: identify the missing detectable yield difference and explain that the known variance, alpha, and desired power cannot determine n without a specified alternative mean/effect. Different target improvements require different sample sizes; smaller improvements generally require more observations under the same model and error requirements. Even if the old-plant variance is provisionally used for the GMO plants, the missing target effect still prevents a unique numerical answer. Recognizing this, correctly interpreting the supplied standard deviation and error/power inputs, and concluding that a target effect must be supplied is eligible for full credit. No invented effect, exact formula, or numerical sample size is required for this path.
Path B — explicitly conditional example: as an EXTRA ASSUMPTION, suppose the 5% price premium motivates choosing a 5% minimum detectable yield improvement, with yield value proportional to kilograms and other costs unchanged. This assumption is not stated by the source. Then mu_target=1.05 kg and delta=0.05 kg. Also assume independent GMO yields with known/planning variance 0.04, a known historical baseline 1 kg, and a one-sided normal-mean test of H0: mu<=1 versus H_A: mu>1. Under this model,
power=Phi(delta sqrt(n)/sigma-z_(1-alpha)),
so n=[(z_(1-alpha)+z_(power))*sigma/delta]^2.
Substituting alpha=0.05, power=0.5, sigma=0.2 and the ASSUMED delta=0.05 gives n=[(1.644854+0)*0.2/0.05]^2=43.288695. Round up to 44 plants; power at 44 is about 0.50537. The source multiple-choice key's 45 is the nearest offered option and a valid conservative choice under these assumptions. Neither 44 nor 45 is uniquely implied by the question as written.
Accept another explicit defensible effect-size/model assumption and any statistically valid, internally consistent power calculation; do not require this particular formula or numerical answer. If the null instead tests whether mean yield exceeds the economic threshold 1.05 kg, a target alternative above that threshold must be specified for the corresponding power calculation: the illustrated test against 1 kg does not establish that yield exceeds 1.05. A silent substitution of a 5% effect cannot earn full credit, even if it happens to produce 44 or 45.

question_text:
Noppo-kun is a hamster that loves books. One day he feels sleepy and wants to buy coffee at Starbook coffee shop. The office hosts two Starbook coffee shops. He wants to know which shop will satisfy his daily dose of caffeine faster. During the next 10 days, he decides to collect data after 5 visits for each shop at different times of the day. The data he collected is as shown below.

|  Visits | Order time at 1st shop (min) | Order time at 2nd shop (min)  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  1 | 1 | 3  |
|  2 | 2 | 1  |
|  3 | 1 | 1  |
|  4 | 3 | 2  |
|  5 | 2 | 1  |
|  Mean | 1.8 | 1.6  |

Let's say you want to do a hypothesis test on this data anyway. Describe the hypothesis ($H_0$ and $H_A$), the null distribution, and the test that should be used. Perform hypothesis testing and conclude according to the data.
canonical_solution:
Let mu_1 and mu_2 be population mean order times for the two shops under comparable target visit conditions. As a primary analysis, use H0: mu_1-mu_2=0 versus H_A: mu_1-mu_2!=0. The recorded visit numbers do not establish matching by time or day, so an independent-sample Welch t-test is a defensible default; equal population variances need not be assumed. Approximate t inference requires independent visits and roughly normal populations for these very small samples. The uncontrolled collection weakens both this model and any causal interpretation.
The sample means are 1.8 and 1.6 minutes. With n_1=n_2=5, sums of squared deviations are 2.8 and 3.2; sample variances are s_1^2=0.7 and s_2^2=0.8 min^2. Thus
SE=sqrt(0.7/5+0.8/5)=sqrt(0.3)=0.547723;
t=(1.8-1.6)/0.547723=0.365148;
nu=(0.7/5+0.8/5)^2 / [(0.7/5)^2/4+(0.8/5)^2/4]=7.964602.
Under H0, the Welch statistic is approximately t_nu. The two-sided p-value is about 0.724507. At an explicitly chosen illustrative alpha=0.05 (not specified in the question), fail to reject H0. A 95% difference interval is approximately [-1.064,1.464] minutes; equivalently |t| is below the approximately 2.308 two-sided critical value. There is insufficient evidence of different mean order times, or of shop 2 reliably being faster; this is not proof that the shops are equal. The observed 0.2-minute advantage for shop 2 is small compared with uncertainty, and possible visit-condition confounding remains.
Accepted alternatives: With an explicit equal-variance assumption, a pooled two-sample t-test has s_p^2=(2.8+3.2)/8=0.75, the same SE and statistic, df=8, and two-sided p about 0.724466. If a directional faster-shop-2 question was specified before looking at the means, H_A: mu_1-mu_2>0 gives one-sided Welch p about 0.362253; the 5% conclusion is unchanged. Reversing subtraction/hypothesis signs consistently is equivalent. Another stated alpha is acceptable when the decision matches it; alpha was not supplied.
A paired test needs an additional, justified matching assumption absent from the source; row numbering or the same visitor alone is not sufficient. Conditionally assuming genuine matched visits, differences (-2,1,0,1,1) have mean 0.2, sample variance 1.7, SE=sqrt(1.7/5)=0.583095, t=0.342997, df=4, and two-sided p about 0.748868. Award full method credit only when this is explicitly conditional on genuine matching, not asserted as established fact. Valid resampling or other formulations may also earn credit when their exchangeability/model assumptions and target of inference are justified; do not silently substitute a different estimand for a mean comparison.

question_text: We observed that, from 1am to 4am, the number of shooting stars in each hour is 8, 4, 3. Assuming that the rate of the falling star follow a Poisson distribution, find the MLE $\hat{\lambda}$.
canonical_solution:

The log likelihood is -3lambda+15 log(lambda)-log(8!4!3!), giving derivative -3+15/lambda=0 and lambda_hat=15/3=5. The second derivative is -15/lambda^2<0, so this is a maximum. question_text: Hamtaro was playing a game with 4 loot boxes. Hamtaro open the boxes 37, 63, 12, 13 times before he won each box. (Hamtaro won on the 38th, 64th, 13th, and 14th tries.) Assume all boxes has the same drop rate, what is the likelihood function of the drop rate $p$?
canonical_solution:
Assume independent Bernoulli trials with a common, constant success probability p and independent boxes, each observed until its first success. If f_i is the number of failures before that success, P(F_i=f_i)=(1-p)^{f_i}p, for f_i=0,1,... . Here f=(37,63,12,13). Therefore
L(p)=product_{i=1}^4 [(1-p)^{f_i}p]=p^4(1-p)^{37+63+12+13}=p^4(1-p)^125, 0<=p<=1.
Equivalently, using success-trial counts t=(38,64,13,14), sum(t_i-1)=129-4=125. There are four successes and 125 failures, not 121 failures. The observed stopping sequences need no binomial combinatorial factor. An expression proportional to this likelihood by a positive p-independent constant, or the equivalent log likelihood 4 log p+125 log(1-p) for 0<p<1, represents the same inferential likelihood.

canonical_solution:
The sample size is UNDERDETERMINED from the source information alone. Planning power requires a target effect size, such as delta=mu_target-mu_0: the mean yield improvement the experiment should be able to detect. The source gives mu_0=1 kg, variance 0.04 kg^2, hence standard deviation sqrt(0.04)=0.2 kg, alpha=0.05, and power=0.5 (beta=0.5). It does not give an explicit target GMO mean or minimum detectable yield improvement. A 5% higher cost is an economic fact, not automatically a 5% statistical yield effect.
Path A — complete underdetermination explanation: identify the missing detectable yield difference and explain that the known variance, alpha, and desired power cannot determine n without a specified alternative mean/effect. Different target improvements require different sample sizes; smaller improvements generally require more observations under the same model and error requirements. Even if the old-plant variance is provisionally used for the GMO plants, the missing target effect still prevents a unique numerical answer. Recognizing this, correctly interpreting the supplied standard deviation and error/power inputs, and concluding that a target effect must be supplied is eligible for full credit. No invented effect, exact formula, or numerical sample size is required for this path.
Path B — explicitly conditional example: as an EXTRA ASSUMPTION, suppose the 5% price premium motivates choosing a 5% minimum detectable yield improvement, with yield value proportional to kilograms and other costs unchanged. Also assume independent GMO yields with known/planning variance 0.04, a known historical baseline 1 kg, and a one-sided normal-mean test of H0: mu<=1 versus H_A: mu>1. Under this model,
power=Phi(delta sqrt(n)/sigma-z_(1-alpha)),
so n=[(z_(1-alpha)+z_(power))*sigma/delta]^2.
Substituting alpha=0.05, power=0.5, sigma=0.2 and the ASSUMED delta=0.05 gives n=[(1.644854+0)*0.2/0.05]^2=43.288695. Round up to 44 plants; power at 44 is about 0.50537. If the null instead tests whether mean yield exceeds the economic threshold 1.05 kg, a target alternative above that threshold must be specified for the corresponding power calculation: the illustrated test against 1 kg does not establish that yield exceeds 1.05. A point estimate above 10%, or a significant test merely against zero, does not establish that the true effect exceeds 10%.
One valid plan fixes the sample size and duration before starting, using an assumed variance/baseline and a target alternative above 10% to achieve a stated power. question_text:
Noppo-kun is a hamster that loves books. One day he feels sleepy and wants to buy coffee at Starbook coffee shop. The office hosts two Starbook coffee shops. He wants to know which shop will satisfy his daily dose of caffeine faster. During the next 10 days, he decides to collect data after 5 visits for each shop at different times of the day. The data he collected is as shown below.

|  Visits | Order time at 1st shop (min) | Order time at 2nd shop (min)  |
| --- | --- | --- |
|  1 | 1 | 3  |
|  2 | 2 | 1  |
|  3 | 1 | 1  |
|  4 | 3 | 2  |
|  5 | 2 | 1  |
|  Mean | 1.8 | 1.6  |

canonical_solution:
Let mu_1 and mu_2 be population mean order times for the two shops under comparable target visit conditions. As a primary analysis, use H0: mu_1-mu_2=0 versus H_A: mu_1-mu_2!=0. The recorded visit numbers do not establish matching by time or day, so an independent-sample Welch t-test is a defensible default; equal population variances need not be assumed. Approximate t inference requires independent visits and roughly normal populations for these very small samples. The uncontrolled collection weakens both this model and any causal interpretation.
The sample means are 1.8 and 1.6 minutes. With n_1=n_2=5, sums of squared deviations are 2.8 and 3.2; sample variances are s_1^2=0.7 and s_2^2=0.8 min^2. Thus
SE=sqrt(0.7/5+0.8/5)=sqrt(0.3)=0.547723;
t=(1.8-1.6)/0.547723=0.365148;
nu=(0.7/5+0.8/5)^2 / [(0.7/5)^2/4+(0.8/5)^2/4]=7.964602.
Under H0, the Welch statistic is approximately t_nu. The two-sided p-value is about 0.724507. At an explicitly chosen illustrative alpha=0.05 (not specified in the question), fail to reject H0. A 95% difference interval is approximately [-1.064,1.464] minutes; equivalently |t| is below the approximately 2.308 two-sided critical value. There is insufficient evidence of different mean order times, or of shop 2 reliably being faster; this is not proof that the shops are equal. The observed 0.2-minute advantage for shop 2 is small compared with uncertainty, and possible visit-condition confounding remains.
Accepted alternatives: With an explicit equal-variance assumption, a pooled two-sample t-test has s_p^2=(2.8+3.2)/8=0.75, the same SE and statistic, df=8, and two-sided p about 0.724466. Reversing subtraction/hypothesis signs consistently is equivalent. Another stated alpha is acceptable when the decision matches it; alpha was not supplied.
A paired test needs an additional, justified matching assumption absent from the source; row numbering or the same visitor alone is not sufficient. Conditionally assuming genuine matched visits, differences (-2,1,0,1,1) have mean 0.2, sample variance 1.7, SE=sqrt(1.7/5)=0.583095, t=0.342997, df=4, and two-sided p about 0.748868. question_text: Hamtaro was playing a game with 4 loot boxes. Hamtaro open the boxes 37, 63, 12, 13 times before he won each box. (Hamtaro won on the 38th, 64th, 13th, and 14th tries.) Assume all boxes has the same drop rate, what is the likelihood function of the drop rate $p$?
canonical_solution:
Assume independent Bernoulli trials with a common, constant success probability p and independent boxes, each observed until its first success. If f_i is the number of failures before that success, P(F_i=f_i)=(1-p)^{f_i}p, for f_i=0,1,... . Here f=(37,63,12,13). Therefore
L(p)=product_{i=1}^4 [(1-p)^{f_i}p]=p^4(1-p)^{37+63+12+13}=p^4(1-p)^125, 0<=p<=1.
Equivalently, using success-trial counts t=(38,64,13,14), sum(t_i-1)=129-4=125. There are four successes and 125 failures, not 121 failures. The observed stopping sequences need no binomial combinatorial factor. An expression proportional to this likelihood by a positive p-independent constant, or the equivalent log likelihood 4 log p+125 log(1-p) for 0<p<1, represents the same inferential likelihood.

nu=(0.7/5+0.8/5)^2 / [(0.7/5)^2/4+(0.8/5)^2/4]=7.964602.

canonical_solution:
The visits were made at different times, but the description does not establish randomized shop assignment or comparable visit-time distributions. Shop choice could be associated with time of day; for example, one shop might be visited near a busy period while the other is visited at a quiet time. This is a possible mechanism, not a fact observed in the table. Merely visiting at different times does not guarantee balanced conditions.
Other unrecorded conditions could include day of week/date, queue length and customer arrival rate, staffing, barista workload, order size/complexity, or promotions. These can affect service time independently of a shop's underlying performance. Without recording, matching, blocking, or randomizing these conditions, a mean difference can combine a shop effect with a difference in demand or order conditions. Define the measured interval consistently (queue-to-order completion or another fixed start/end); the table's 'order time' does not specify every measurement detail.
The same hamster provides only five visits per shop in ten days, so precision is low and generalization to other times, customers, and orders is limited. Small sample size itself mainly increases uncertainty; it is not proof of systematic bias. Visit numbers are not evidence of matched same-day/same-condition pairs, and repeated visits may have dependence. The data do not prove any named confounder actually occurred. A stronger future design could randomize and balance shop visits within comparable time/day blocks, standardize orders and timing definitions, and record workload/queue conditions; proposing a redesign is useful but not required to answer the flaws question.

question_text: Koshi-kun creates a new GMO sunflower plant which he claims to have better yield. canonical_solution:
The sample size is UNDERDETERMINED from the source information alone. Planning power requires a target effect size, such as delta=mu_target-mu_0: the mean yield improvement the experiment should be able to detect. The source gives mu_0=1 kg, variance 0.04 kg^2, hence standard deviation sqrt(0.04)=0.2 kg, alpha=0.05, and power=0.5 (beta=0.5). It does not give an explicit target GMO mean or minimum detectable yield improvement. A 5% higher cost is an economic fact, not automatically a 5% statistical yield effect.
Path A — complete underdetermination explanation: identify the missing detectable yield difference and explain that the known variance, alpha, and desired power cannot determine n without a specified alternative mean/effect. Different target improvements require different sample sizes; smaller improvements generally require more observations under the same model and error requirements. Even if the old-plant variance is provisionally used for the GMO plants, the missing target effect still prevents a unique numerical answer. Recognizing this, correctly interpreting the supplied standard deviation and error/power inputs, and concluding that a target effect must be supplied is eligible for full credit. No invented effect, exact formula, or numerical sample size is required for this path.
Path B — explicitly conditional example: as an EXTRA ASSUMPTION, suppose the 5% price premium motivates choosing a 5% minimum detectable yield improvement, with yield value proportional to kilograms and other costs unchanged. This assumption is not stated by the source. Then mu_target=1.05 kg and delta=0.05 kg. Also assume independent GMO yields with known/planning variance 0.04, a known historical baseline 1 kg, and a one-sided normal-mean test of H0: mu<=1 versus H_A: mu>1. Under this model,
power=Phi(delta sqrt(n)/sigma-z_(1-alpha)),

Choose one primary outcome before the experiment and define the experimental unit and observation window. A defensible choice is mean 24-hour "Read more" clicks per assigned post, compared between link-in-post and link-in-comment treatments. question_text: Hamtaro was playing a game with 4 loot boxes. Hamtaro open the boxes 37, 63, 12, 13 times before he won each box. (Hamtaro won on the 38th, 64th, 13th, and 14th tries.) Assume all boxes has the same drop rate, what is the likelihood function of the drop rate $p$?
canonical_solution:
Assume independent Bernoulli trials with a common, constant success probability p and independent boxes, each observed until its first success. If f_i is the number of failures before that success, P(F_i=f_i)=(1-p)^{f_i}p, for f_i=0,1,... . Here f=(37,63,12,13). Therefore
L(p)=product_{i=1}^4 [(1-p)^{f_i}p]=p^4(1-p)^{37+63+12+13}=p^4(1-p)^125, 0<=p<=1.
Equivalently, using success-trial counts t=(38,64,13,14), sum(t_i-1)=129-4=125. There are four successes and 125 failures, not 121 failures. The observed stopping sequences need no binomial combinatorial factor. An expression proportional to this likelihood by a positive p-independent constant, or the equivalent log likelihood 4 log p+125 log(1-p) for 0<p<1, represents the same inferential likelihood.

Let's say you want to do a hypothesis test on this data anyway. Describe the hypothesis ($H_0$ and $H_A$), the null distribution, and the test that should be used. Perform hypothesis testing and conclude according to the data.
canonical_solution:
Let mu_1 and mu_2 be population mean order times for the two shops under comparable target visit conditions. As a primary analysis, use H0: mu_1-mu_2=0 versus H_A: mu_1-mu_2!=0. The recorded visit numbers do not establish matching by time or day, so an independent-sample Welch t-test is a defensible default; equal population variances need not be assumed. Approximate t inference requires independent visits and roughly normal populations for these very small samples. The uncontrolled collection weakens both this model and any causal interpretation.
The sample means are 1.8 and 1.6 minutes. With n_1=n_2=5, sums of squared deviations are 2.8 and 3.2; sample variances are s_1^2=0.7 and s_2^2=0.8 min^2. Thus
SE=sqrt(0.7/5+0.8/5)=sqrt(0.3)=0.547723;
t=(1.8-1.6)/0.547723=0.365148;
nu=(0.7/5+0.8/5)^2 / [(0.7/5)^2/4+(0.8/5)^2/4]=7.964602.
Under H0, the Welch statistic is approximately t_nu. The two-sided p-value is about 0.724507. At an explicitly chosen illustrative alpha=0.05 (not specified in the question), fail to reject H0. A 95% difference interval is approximately [-1.064,1.464] minutes; equivalently |t| is below the approximately 2.308 two-sided critical value. There is insufficient evidence of different mean order times, or of shop 2 reliably being faster; this is not proof that the shops are equal. The observed 0.2-minute advantage for shop 2 is small compared with uncertainty, and possible visit-condition confounding remains.
Accepted alternatives: With an explicit equal-variance assumption, a pooled two-sample t-test has s_p^2=(2.8+3.2)/8=0.75, the same SE and statistic, df=8, and two-sided p about 0.724466. If a directional faster-shop-2 question was specified before looking at the means, H_A: mu_1-mu_2>0 gives one-sided Welch p about 0.362253; the 5% conclusion is unchanged.
